links.outcome: Sensitivity for DR and AMD when AI-negative images skip clinician review versus human-only reading
links.effect: DR sensitivity fell 0.9168 to 0.8838 (diff -0.0330; p<0.001); AMD 0.8570 to 0.8445 (diff -0.0124; p=0.008); ophthalmologist review reduced to 7.3%-16.8% of images.
links.quote: For DR, mean sensitivity decreased from 0.9168 to 0.8838 (difference, -0.0330; 95% CI, -0.0495 to -0.0165; p < 0.001), whereas the increase in specificity did not reach statistical significance.

links.outcome: AI-assisted negative-screening workflow versus human-only reading on same images: sensitivity, specificity, workload
links.effect: Workload cut to 7.3%-8.0% (DR), 11.7%-11.9% (RVO), 13.5%-16.8% (AMD); sensitivity lower for DR and AMD, unchanged for RVO; specificity not significantly changed.
links.quote: Thus, the MRMC analysis showed a significant sensitivity trade-off for DR and AMD, with no statistically significant specificity gain, while RVO performance was preserved.

links.outcome: Human-AI team performance in intended deployment mode, including automation bias
links.effect: Study simulated triage on reader outputs obtained without AI access, so it could not assess real-time reader behavior, anchoring or overreliance; these were left to prospective studies.
links.quote: Therefore, the diagnostic performance estimated in this study should be interpreted as a workflow-level simulation under fixed reader decisions, rather than as the prospective performance of an interactive human-AI system.

links.outcome: Effect of a more conservative operating threshold (0.995 vs 0.99) on sensitivity and review workload
links.effect: For DR, sensitivity rose to 0.85-0.94 with review up modestly (7-8% to 8-9%); for AMD little sensitivity gain but review rose from 14-17% to 18-22%; RVO unchanged.
links.quote: For AMD, the same change yielded little sensitivity gain but a larger increase in review burden (about 14%–17% to 18%–22%), and RVO sensitivity was unchanged.

links.outcome: False negatives from out-of-distribution or atypical pathology outside the AI's target disease scope
links.effect: Composite false negatives included myopic chorioretinal atrophy, geographic atrophy, and treatment-altered DR; AI negatives were appropriate within scope but missed out-of-distribution pathology.
links.quote: While such classifications were appropriate within the algorithm’s defined scope, this discrepancy highlights a potential limitation of disease-specific AI models in negative-screening workflows, particularly when encountering out-of-distribution retinal pathologies.

links.outcome: Generalizability of performance beyond single tertiary center and exclusion of ambiguous cases
links.effect: Discordant cases excluded (AMD 6.1%-11.6%); AMD full-cohort referral burden 19.6% versus 13.5%-16.8% in reader-agreed sets; results may overestimate performance.
links.quote: The primary AMD estimates should therefore be interpreted as results for reader-agreed cases rather than definitive performance in a full screening population containing ambiguous findings.

unlisted_practices: AI negative-screening triage gate with disease-specific operating thresholds to reduce specialist workload
uncertainty-based referral or selective review of borderline AI-negative cases (proposed)

links.outcome: Missed disease when AI-negative outputs substituted for diagnosis
links.effect: DR sensitivity decreased 0.9168 to 0.8838 (difference -0.0330; p < 0.001); AMD 0.8570 to 0.8445 (difference -0.0124; p = 0.008).
links.quote: AI-assisted negative-screening can reduce ophthalmologist workload across multiple retinal diseases, but with disease-specific safety trade-offs: because AI-negative images are not reviewed, reduced sensitivity for DR and AMD means a small proportion of true-positive cases would go undetected, potentially delaying diagnosis and treatment for sight-threatening disease.

links.outcome: Sensitivity loss when AI-negative images bypassed review
links.effect: Composite sensitivity decreased 0.9122 to 0.9039 (difference -0.0083; p < 0.001) while review burden fell to 27.7%-30.1%.
links.quote: This trade-off is clinically important because, in the present negative-screening workflow, AI-negative images were classified directly as negative and were not reviewed by ophthalmologists; therefore, any false-negative triage decision constituted a missed positive case within the workflow itself.

links.outcome: diagnostic sensitivity under AI-assisted negative-screening triage
links.effect: Sensitivity decreased for DR (0.9168 to 0.8838, p < 0.001) and AMD (0.8570 to 0.8445, p = 0.008), was unchanged for RVO (0.9807, p = 1.000), and decreased for composite disease (0.9122 to 0.9039, p < 0.001).
